item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Israel pitched advanced drones to UAE, leaked emails reveal: Report
item.description:
Israel pitched advanced drones to UAE, leaked emails reveal: Report

Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 08/03/2026 - 19:26
The UAE escalated its request for Israeli drones following a Houthi missile and drone attack in 2022
The Elbit Systems UK stand is pictured on the opening day of the Farnborough International Airshow 2026 in Farnborough, south-west of London, on 20 July 2026 (Toby Shepheard/AFP)
Off

The UAE secretly pushed for the sale of Israeli drones by Elbit Systems following an attack on Abu Dhabi by Yemen’s Houthis in 2022, according to leaked emails reported by Haaretz and Drop Site News.

Emails dating from 2021 through early 2023 reveal that Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest defence contractor, had already begun discussing the sale of Hermes 900 drones, SkyEye wide-area surveillance sensors, ground control equipment, training, and logistical support.

The sale was described as “urgent” after the Houthis in Yemen launched a missile and drone attack on Abu Dhabi on 17 January 2022.

The emails from Elbit Systems’ executives were obtained by Handala, an online hacking group, with supposed links to the Iranian government. They were verified by both Haaretz and Drop Site News.

The initial drone sale was valued at $154m, with additional upgrades bringing it up to $225m. The leaked correspondence didn’t reveal whether the drones were delivered.

SkyEye sensors comprise electro-optical cameras that allow a drone to record a vast area in real time at high resolution. The footage can be rewound through multiple viewpoints to trace objects back to their place of origin.

UAE and Israel established fund for joint defence acquisition, sources say
Read More »

The Hermes 900 is an advanced Israeli reconnaissance and surveillance drone that has a payload of up to 990 pounds. According to reports, it can carry up to eight surface-to-air missiles.

The emails revealed that in March 2022 the head of research and development at the Israeli defence ministry's arms development directorate was travelling to the UAE with a proposal to sell Hermes 900 drones with "an operational solution for maintaining surveillance beyond the country's borders – detecting missile and drone launches into the country”.

At the time, the UAE had just suffered a missile and drone attack that targeted oil tanker trucks and the Abu Dhabi airport.

The UAE normalised relations with Israel approximately two years before, under the Abraham Accords. That agreement, brokered by Trump's first administration, was framed as an effort to bolster defence ties between Israel and the UAE, Bahrain and Morocco.

The emails also contain two references to the SkyStriker loitering munition and another drone, the Hermes 650.

The emails provide a rare window into the close defence ties between the UAE and Israel, along with the specific Israeli armaments and technical systems that analysts have long said entice Gulf states.

The UAE is one of the closest Arab and Muslim states to Israel, and joined it and the US in launching hundreds of strikes on Iran.

Middle East Eye revealed in May that Israel and the UAE have established a joint defence fund to acquire new weapons systems amid the war on Iran.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Pentagon is emailing military experts and asking best way to 'punish' Iran: Report
item.description:
Pentagon is emailing military experts and asking best way to 'punish' Iran: Report

Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 08/03/2026 - 18:47
Is the Trump administration's strategy hinging on crowdsourcing ideas?
The Pentagon, which houses the US Department of War, is seen from above in Arlington, Virginia, on 3 March 2022 (Joshua Roberts/Reuters)
Off

The Trump administration seems to be struggling to figure out how to get out of its self-made Iran quagmire.

According to a CNN report on Monday, the US military is now crowdsourcing ideas among military experts for what to do next in order to push Iran into a deal that is to President Donald Trump's liking. 

"We are looking for new creative and unconventional ways to pressure and punish Iran," an email from an officer in US Central Command's (Centcom) intelligence branch read last week, according to the CNN report.

A Centcom spokesperson said the move is not unusual, and that it "has a long history of thinking and working in innovative ways".

But the email suggests the Pentagon did not plan for the conflict to drag out this long.

The on-again, off-again US-Israeli war on Iran, which began on 28 February, led to Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which has sent energy prices skyrocketing and directly impacted Trump voters. 

On Sunday, Saudi Arabia's state media said Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had spoken to Trump over the phone, and reportedly stressed "the necessity of prioritising dialogue to de-escalate tensions and the importance of exerting all possible efforts to achieve a truce, which paves the way for diplomatic solutions".

Talks

Iran has denied that any talks are ongoing with the US despite a claim by Trump, who called off strikes on the country on Saturday. 

Iran denies talks with US as Trump halts strikes at the last minute
Read More »

Trump announced that negotiations with Iran would begin on Monday after he decided to hold off on new strikes against the Islamic Republic in order to pursue a deal.

"Obviously, they don't want to be attacked," Trump told reporters on Sunday on board Air Force One.

"Now what we're doing is we're talking to them in the form of a negotiation. It begins tomorrow afternoon."

However, Iran's foreign ministry has said there were currently no negotiations with the US but that talks were taking place with Oman over the Strait of Hormuz. 

The foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said discussions with Oman were "constructive" and aimed at reaching an agreement on a new route.

"We are not currently negotiating with the United States. Our negotiations are with Oman to secure passage through the Strait of Hormuz," Baghaei said during a press briefing. 

"We hope that both regional and extra-regional actors will appreciate this responsible move by Iran and adopt a constructive approach."

He added that as long as a US naval blockade on Iranian ports continues, "the situation in the Strait of Hormuz will remain unchanged".

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Drone strike on North Darfur court kills at least 35, rights group says
item.description:
Drone strike on North Darfur court kills at least 35, rights group says

Submitted by Victoria Amani Mwaniki Kishoiyian on Mon, 08/03/2026 - 21:29
The attack comes amid heightened Sudanese army drone operations across Darfur
Protesters in Warsaw, Poland, hold placards during a protest against the Rapid Support Forces committing mass atrocities in the Darfur region of Sudan, on 8 November 2025 (Neil Milton/Reuters)
Off

On Sunday, a drone strike, purportedly carried out by the Sudanese army, targeted Sudan's Customary Court in al-Zawiya Ghara, killing at least 35 people and injuring others. 

All the victims were inside the court building and its immediate surroundings when the attack occurred, according to the Emergency Lawyers Group, which monitors violence against civilians in Sudan. 

Al-Zawiya Ghara is one of many villages in North Darfur state controlled by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). 

The drone fired at least four missiles at the court building while local leaders conducted a meeting. 

Among the dead are two RSF field commanders, four tribal elders, and traditional leaders hailing from the Mahameed branch of the Rizeigat, according to the Sudan Tribune.   

Sunday's attack comes amid heightened Sudanese army drone operations across Darfur, closing in on RSF positions to weaken the paramilitary group after successive defeats in North Kordofan. 

The largely RSF-dominated Sudan Founding Coalition, known as Tasis, blamed the Sudanese army for the strike.

In the Sudan Tribune, a Tasis spokesperson, Ahmed Tugod Lisan, urged an independent investigation to hold those responsible to account. 

The Emergency Lawyers Group has demanded an investigation into the drone strike and denounced the targeting of the court, deeming attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure a “grave violation of international humanitarian law”.

It further stated that drones are increasingly used to target civilian areas and gatherings, exacerbating the risks faced by the population. 

The RSF also stands accused of committing war crimes, including carrying out drone strikes on civilians over the past three years of the war. 

The paramilitary group’s siege on el-Fasher, one of Darfur’s largest cities, in October of 2025, bore the “hallmarks of genocide” per a United Nations fact-finding mission. 

RSF commanders sentenced

In early July, the anti-terrorism and crimes against the state court in Port Sudan sentenced RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, and 15 other defendants to death in absentia. 

UK hosting 'discreet' Sudan event featuring UAE-aligned RSF representatives
Read More »

According to the Sudan Tribune, they were convicted of their roles in the killing of West Darfur Governor Khamis Abdullah Abakar, crimes against humanity, war crimes, prohibited warfare, and genocide in el-Geneina.

Presided over by special judge Mohamed al-Amin, the ruling constitutes the first judicial conviction of the paramilitary group’s leadership since the outbreak of Sudan’s war on 15 April 2023. 

The trial centred heavily on the 2023 assassination of Governor Abakar, a day after he denounced an RSF shelling on the el-Jamarik neighbourhood.

Human Rights Watch concluded in 2024 that actions in the capital of West Darfur, el-Geneina, constituted ethnic cleansing and possibly genocide against the Masalit people and other non-Arab communities. 

Although video footage circulated online of Abakar’s body being mutilated by known RSF soldiers, the paramilitary group repeatedly blamed the Sudanese Armed Forces and denied responsibility. 

Middle East Eye reported in June 2023 that around 1,500 people were killed in el-Geneina in the first two months of the war, forcing tens of thousands of Masalit residents to flee el-Geneina and West Darfur on foot to seek refuge across the border in eastern Chad. 

Among the trial’s defendants were two brothers of Hemedti: RSF deputy leader Abdel Rahim Hamdan Dagalo and Algoney Hamdan Daglo Musa, also known as al-Qoni.

The court also handed down convictions to Abdel Rahman Juma Barkallah, the RSF commander in West Darfur, and al-Tijani al-Tahir Karshoum, the state’s former deputy governor. 

The court held Hemedti legally responsible for directing the genocide of the Masalit and siege of el-Geneina, citing the systematic destruction and looting of property, as well as deliberate attacks on civilians, residential areas, schools, and places of worship. 

Dagalo was convicted of co-organising the siege of el-Geneina, the civilian displacement, and the genocide of the Masalit.

Qoni was found liable for facilitating the siege, while Barkallah was liable for leading frontline RSF soldiers during systematic assaults on Masalit neighbourhoods. 

The court ordered the confiscation of all RSF assets and instructed the state to request Interpol red notices to secure the arrest and extradition of those convicted.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Israel revels in Spain's migrant crisis while embarrassing ally Morocco
item.description:
Israel revels in Spain's migrant crisis while embarrassing ally Morocco

Submitted by Elis Gjevori on Sun, 08/02/2026 - 16:19
Israel and the US exploited the deaths of Moroccan migrants to punish Spain for its stance on Gaza and Iran
A woman sits by a barbed-wire fence as relatives await the return of people from Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta at the Bab Sebta border crossing near Fnideq, Morocco, 2 August 2026 (Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP)
Off

Israeli political leaders have mocked and exploited the migration crisis engulfing Morocco, an Israeli ally, and Spain, whose relations with Israel have sharply deteriorated.

Israel's ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, wrote on X last week with barely concealed glee: "Spain, which never misses an opportunity to lecture Israel, has declared a state of emergency in Ceuta following the crisis over its immigration policy."

Spain did not declare a state of emergency in Ceuta.

Danon's real grievance appears to be Madrid's forceful and consistent condemnation of Israel's genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, along with its refusal to back the US and Israel in their war against Iran.

"The involvement of official Israeli channels and associated social media accounts in amplifying anti-Spanish rhetoric in the wake of the Ceuta crisis seeks to undermine Spanish strategic positions in the Middle East and North Africa region," Denis Cenusa, a geopolitical analyst and fellow at the Centre for European Policy Analysis, told Middle East Eye.

"This constitutes clear retaliation for Spain's firm stance on the Palestinian cause and the joint US-Israeli attacks against Iran," he added.

More than 60,000 Moroccan migrants attempted to cross from Morocco into Ceuta, a Spanish enclave in North Africa.

At least 70 drowned or were crushed in the attempt, a number expected to rise.

'Why did they open the doors'

Among the dead was Moroccan footballer Faten Ben Omar El Azizi, who played for Moghreb Atletico Tetuan.

"The youth are lost… Who opened the door the first time? Why did they open it so that our children could be killed?" her mother said in a video published by Al Ayoum 24, shortly before Faten was buried in a Tetouan cemetery.

Beyond the grief inflicted on her family, El Azizi's death exposed an uncomfortable truth about the country she represented.

Morocco has emerged as something of a footballing powerhouse in recent years: its men's national team ranks sixth in the world, and the state has poured millions of dollars into developing the women's game.

El Azizi belonged to the generation that investment was supposed to benefit.  

Thousands make dramatic sea crossing into Ceuta from Morocco
Read More »

That investment into the country's human capital looks harder to square with what happened next.

According to several reports, the Moroccan state, headed by King Mohammed VI, opened the border gates into Ceuta, known in Morocco as Sabtah, last Thursday.

The message to many Moroccans was unmistakable that the route out of the country and into Spanish territory was open.

Madrid has so far avoided publicly blaming Rabat, but a source close to Spain's foreign ministry told MEE that officials privately believe the Moroccan state deliberately orchestrated the crisis.

Spanish authorities received intelligence about a possible surge in crossings into Ceuta and Melilla ahead of Morocco's Throne Day but failed to act, the Spanish outlet The Objective reported on Saturday.

Military and civilian intelligence sources told the outlet that officials repeatedly disregarded warnings, including alerts issued only days before the mass movement began.

Observers had already recorded an unusual influx of buses into Fnideq, the Moroccan town closest to Ceuta, before thousands of people converged on the border and crossed into the enclave.

'Spain will pay a price'

What Morocco has actually gained from all this remains unclear, beyond politically wounding Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, whose relationship with Washington has also deteriorated.

Sanchez may well have believed he'd secured lasting peace with Rabat after a diplomatic rupture that ran from December 2020 to March 2022. 

Fifty years of plunder: How Morocco and its allies profit from Western Sahara
Read More »

In March 2022 he wrote to Mohammed VI endorsing Morocco's autonomy proposal for Western Sahara, a major shift in Spain's position on the decades-old dispute.

A year later he helped bring Morocco into the joint Spanish-Portuguese bid to host the 2030 World Cup, and let the king unveil Morocco's inclusion through his own minister, Chakib Benmoussa. The alliance appears to have been jeopardised by Morocco for reasons no one has yet explained.

Before many of the bodies had even been recovered from the sea, Israel's national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir, offered his "congratulations" to Sanchez "for his profound commitment to welcoming immigration and 'human diversity'."

He added: "As someone who demonstrates great concern for Hamas and the residents of Gaza, I call on you to translate words into actions: open the doors of Spain and grant refuge to the residents of Gaza who seek to emigrate."

The intervention wasn't aimed at Spain alone. By turning dead Moroccans into ammunition against Madrid, Israeli officials also humiliated a government that normalised ties with Israel on 22 December 2020 and has treated that relationship as a source of diplomatic leverage ever since.

Israel and the US have both started questioning Spain's hold over Ceuta and Melilla altogether.

Earlier this year, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, wanted for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, accused Sanchez's government of waging a "diplomatic war" and warned it would not be allowed to continue "without paying an immediate price."

Spanish commentators accuse Israel and US of involvement in Ceuta crisis
Read More »

"Israel will not remain silent in the face of those who attack us," he said.

Many analysts now suspect this was that price.

"The Israeli ambassador to the UN and unofficial accounts on X have been amplifying anti-colonial rhetoric directed against Spain. Their emergence coincided with the height of the crisis, which could indicate a degree of coordination," geopolitical analyst Cenusa said.

In Washington, a House Appropriations Committee report published on 30 April described Ceuta and Melilla as Spanish-controlled cities "located in Moroccan territory" and urged the secretary of state to push negotiations over their status.

The wording appeared only in a report attached to the bill, not the bill itself, but it read as a signal to Spain, a Nato member. The House passed the legislation on 15 July; the Senate has not, and the president has not signed it.

No hard evidence has emerged that Israel, the US and Morocco coordinated the crisis. However, with Israeli leaders openly gloating on social media, at least one member of Sanchez’s government has entertained the possibility.

Spanish Transport Minister Oscar Puente shared a post stating: "Some in Washington, Tel Aviv, and Rabat... wanted images of our security forces and armed forces machine-gunning children on the beach."
